summary: Describes the architecture of Segment Routing (SR) policies. An SR Policy is an ordered list of segments, which are instructions, that steers packet flows along a chosen path using source routing. Packets are steered into a policy at a headend node, so intermediate routers do not need per-path state. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: An SR Policy tells a headend router which ordered set of network instructions to apply to selected traffic. The router chooses a valid candidate path, checks its segments, and steers matching packets onto that path.

what is drop upon invalid in segment routing
subtitle: How a headend selects and uses segment lists to steer traffic along a chosen path.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing provides source routing, but deployments need defined rules for identifying policies, validating paths, choosing a path, and steering traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A policy is identified by headend, color, and endpoint. It holds candidate paths made of segment lists, and the headend selects the highest-preference valid path for forwarding.
tldr.outcome: The architecture applies to SR-MPLS and SRv6 and updates RFC 8402. It specifies concepts and behavior rather than defining new protocol extensions.

today: RFC 9256 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2022 and updates RFC 8402. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Segment Routing Policies
sections.content:
Segment Routing lets a headend place ordered instructions, called segments, into a packet. Intermediate routers follow those instructions without keeping per-path state.

An SR Policy is an ordered list of segments used to steer a flow for a particular purpose. RFC 9256 details policy identity, candidate paths, and steering for both SR-MPLS and SRv6, updating RFC 8402.
sections.plainLanguage: The headend router chooses a route and places its instructions in the packet. Other routers follow those instructions without storing a separate route for each flow.

sections.title: Policy Identity and Candidate Paths
sections.content:
An SR Policy is identified by the tuple <Headend, Color, Endpoint>. The headend is the node where the policy is applied, the endpoint is its destination, and the non-zero 32-bit color associates it with an intent or objective.

A policy has one or more candidate paths. A path may be explicit, computed dynamically from objectives and constraints, or composite, grouping other policies. Candidate paths have their own identity tuple: Protocol-Origin, Originator, and Discriminator. A symbolic name is for display, not identification.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy's identity says where it starts, what it is for, and where it ends. It can hold several possible paths, each identified by its source and identifiers rather than by the segment list alone.

sections.title: Selecting the Active Path
sections.content:
A candidate path is usable when it is valid. The active path is the valid path with the highest Preference; the default Preference is 100, and a higher value wins. The headend reruns selection when a path is added, removed, changed, or changes validity.

Ties are resolved first by the higher Protocol-Origin, then an optional preference for the installed path, then the lower Originator, and finally the higher Discriminator. An SR Policy is valid when at least one candidate path is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The headend uses the valid path with the highest Preference. If paths tie, fixed tie-break rules select one so the result does not depend on arrival order.

sections.title: Segment Types and Lists
sections.content:
A segment list is an ordered sequence. Types A and B carry a ready SR-MPLS label or SRv6 SID. Types C through K describe prefixes or link adjacencies that the headend resolves using its Segment Routing Database.

The first segment becomes the top label or first SRv6 SID. When a segment type permits an optional algorithm and none is specified, the headend should use Strict Shortest Path if available, otherwise the default Shortest Path algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: A segment can name a ready-to-use instruction or describe a prefix or link that the headend must resolve. The first segment is the first instruction applied to the packet.

sections.title: Path Validity and Binding SIDs
sections.content:
An explicit segment list is invalid if it is empty, has weight zero, mixes SR-MPLS and SRv6 types, or cannot be resolved as required. A dynamic path is invalid if its objective and constraints have no solution; a composite path is valid when at least one constituent policy is valid.

A Binding SID (BSID) can represent a policy path in forwarding. Candidate paths for one policy should share a BSID, while different policies must not. A valid policy installs a BSID-keyed forwarding entry when the value is available.
sections.plainLanguage: The headend checks that a path can be resolved before using it. A Binding SID gives forwarding a single identifier for the selected policy path.

sections.title: Steering Traffic into a Policy
sections.content:
A headend can steer traffic by a packet's active SID matching a local BSID, by a BGP or service route that resolves through a policy, by per-flow selection, or through a local routing policy. BGP color and endpoint can select a matching policy, and an authorized local policy can trigger a dynamic path on demand.

When a policy becomes invalid, default behavior removes it from forwarding and uses the ordinary forwarding table. Drop-Upon-Invalid instead keeps the policy with a drop action. Optional color-only modes specify fallback searches before the headend uses the IGP path.
sections.plainLanguage: The headend can select a policy from a route, a packet classification, or local configuration. If the policy fails, traffic normally uses ordinary routing, unless Drop-Upon-Invalid is configured.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The security considerations of the SR architecture and its SR-MPLS and SRv6 specifications apply. If multiple nodes advertise the same policy endpoint, traffic may be diverted to an unintended node. An incorrect BGP color can also steer traffic onto an unintended path.

Symbolic names are externally supplied text and may be inaccurate; implementations should rely on policy identifiers. RFC 9256 creates a Segment Types subregistry with initial entries A through K.
sections.plainLanguage: A duplicate endpoint or incorrect color can send traffic along an unintended route. Treat displayed names as labels and check the policy's actual identifiers.
